notes.b: Pure water contains a very small number of ions, produced when water molecules transfer protons to each other.
points: Pure water conducts electricity very slightly, so it must contain a small number of ions.

These ions come from the self-ionisation (auto-ionisation) of water, in which one water molecule donates a proton to another; this is a Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction: H₂O(l) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
In simplified form: H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
The equilibrium lies very far to the left: at 25 °C only about 2 in every 1000 million (1.8 × 10⁻⁹) water molecules are ionised at any moment.
In pure water each ionisation gives one H₃O⁺ and one OH⁻, so [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻].
A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], acidic when [H⁺] > [OH⁻], and basic (alkaline) when [H⁺] < [OH⁻]; even acidic solutions contain some OH⁻ and basic solutions contain some H⁺.
Step 1: Write the equilibrium constant for H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻: Kc = [H⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [H₂O].
Step 2: So little water ionises that [H₂O] is effectively constant: 1000 g of water per litre ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 55.6 mol L⁻¹.
Step 3: Combine the two constants: Kc × [H₂O] = [H⁺][OH⁻]. This new constant is the ionic product of water, Kw.
Definition: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻], or in simplified form Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]; it is the product of the hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion concentrations.
At 25 °C, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ (units mol² L⁻², often omitted).
Pure water at 25 °C has [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺]² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
Therefore [H⁺] = √(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹.
So pH = −log₁₀(1.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 7.0, which is why pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C.
Kw applies to every dilute aqueous solution, not just pure water: if [H⁺] rises, [OH⁻] falls so that the product stays 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Example: a solution with [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ (pH 2) has [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² mol L⁻¹.
Taking −log₁₀ of Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] gives pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C, where pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; this is used for bases in “pH calculations”.

notes.h: Temperature dependence of Kw (Higher Level only)
points: Self-ionisation is endothermic in the forward direction (ΔH about +56 kJ mol⁻¹); it is the reverse of neutralisation, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, which is exothermic.
By Le Châtelier's principle, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, the endothermic direction, producing more H⁺ and OH⁻, so Kw increases; cooling decreases Kw.
Like every equilibrium constant, Kw changes only with temperature; that is why Kw values are quoted with a temperature.
Kw at 0 °C is 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, giving a neutral pH of 7.47.
Kw at 25 °C is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving a neutral pH of 7.00.
Kw at 50 °C is 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving a neutral pH of 6.63.
Kw at 100 °C is 5.1 × 10⁻¹³, giving a neutral pH of 6.14.
Hot pure water has a pH below 7 but is still neutral, because [H⁺] and [OH⁻] increase equally and stay equal; neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not pH = 7.
The neutral pH is therefore lower at higher temperatures and higher at lower temperatures.

keyTerms.definition: The reaction in which one water molecule transfers a proton to another, producing a very small amount of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
The H₃O⁺ ion formed when a water molecule accepts a proton; it is often written simply as H⁺(aq) in equations.
The constant Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] for water and dilute aqueous solutions, equal to 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
A solution in which [H⁺] is greater than [OH⁻].
A solution in which [H⁺] is less than [OH⁻]; also called alkaline.
A reaction that takes in heat energy from its surroundings.

questions.prompt: Write an equation for the self-ionisation of water and explain why pure water is described as neutral.
questions.model: The self-ionisation of water is H₂O(l) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), or simply H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Each ionisation produces one H₃O⁺ and one OH⁻, so in pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]. A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻]; it is acidic when [H⁺] > [OH⁻] and basic when [H⁺] < [OH⁻]. Pure water is therefore neutral, even though only about 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ of its molecules are ionised at 25 °C.

questions.prompt: Define the ionic product of water, Kw. Kw at 25 °C is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Show that the pH of pure water at 25 °C is 7.0, and calculate [OH⁻] in a solution with [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹.
questions.model: Kw is the ionic product of water, the product of the hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion concentrations: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = [H⁺][OH⁻]. In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺]² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Therefore [H⁺] = √(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹, and pH = −log₁₀(1.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 7.0. For [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹: [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol L⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Kw is 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 50 °C. Explain why Kw increases with temperature, calculate the pH of pure water at 50 °C, and explain whether this water is acidic.
questions.model: Self-ionisation is endothermic in the forward direction, so by Le Châtelier's principle a rise in temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, producing more H⁺ and OH⁻ and increasing Kw. In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺] = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.35 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹. pH = −log₁₀(2.35 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.63. The water is not acidic: [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so it is neutral, even though its pH is below 7.
